title: Heaps of jewels (section 24)
hook: jewels piled high as mountains are less than keeping four lines

segments.voice: Yesterday: equal. The teaching is level, with nothing high or low in it. Your line: no high, no low. Did you speak to someone as an equal, without looking up or past? Day one thousand one hundred forty-one.

A woman leaves her bag on a train: wallet, phone, keys, the ring she took off to wash her hands. Gone. That night, unable to sleep, she finds herself saying a poem she learned as a girl, every line still there. The train took everything she was carrying in her hands. It couldn't touch what she was carrying by heart. Section twenty-four of the Diamond Sutra sets those two kinds of keeping side by side, and it doesn't hold back on the size of the pile. Today: heaps of jewels.
screen: `A BAG LEFT ON A TRAIN.` → `A POEM STILL THERE.` → `TWO KINDS OF KEEPING.`

segments.voice: First, the heap. The Buddha describes someone who piles up the seven precious things, gold, silver and the rest, in heaps as high as all the Sumeru mountains in a vast world system, and gives them all away. Sumeru, in Buddhist cosmology, is the great mountain at the center of a world. So this is a gift the size of a mountain range, made of treasure. Second, the four lines. Then someone else takes this teaching of the perfection of wisdom, even just four lines of it, keeps it, recites it, and explains it to others. That's all. A short verse, held and shared. Third, the scale. The merit of the mountain of jewels, the Buddha says, is not a hundredth part of the merit of the four lines. Not even the tiniest share. Not any fraction you could name or find a comparison for. The sutra pushes the numbers until numbers give up. Fourth, why. We've heard this comparison before in the sutra, but today's picture makes the reason plain. Jewels can be given once, and then they're gone, or lost, or fought over. Four lines kept by heart travel with a person through sleepless nights and hospital waiting rooms, and when they're explained to someone else, nobody has less. This whole week, the sutra has been taking things away: no grasping the mind, no merit to own, no perfect body, nothing to teach, nothing gained, no high or low. And then it hands back something small enough to carry anywhere: a few lines, by heart.
screen: `JEWELS HIGH AS SUMERU.` · `FOUR LINES, KEPT AND SHARED.` · `NOT A HUNDREDTH PART.` · `WHAT A TRAIN CAN'T TAKE.` · then, large: `LESS THAN FOUR LINES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: keep four lines by heart. This week has already handed you some. Here are four of its lines: can't be grasped. So-called merit. Not the least thing. No high, no low. Settle, and breathe. Say the first line silently on one out-breath. Then the second. Then the third and fourth. Now try them again without help, in order. If one slips, wait a breath and let it come back on its own; if it doesn't, that's all right. Go round again, a little slower. By the bell, they may be yours to carry without a page. The bell holds the time.
Heaps of jewels. In section twenty-four, treasure piled as high as mountains gives less merit than keeping and sharing four lines of this teaching. Today's word.

Your line: less than four lines. This week ends here. Today, say this week's four lines once more before sleep, and if it feels right, share them with one person. Day one thousand one hundred forty-one.

howItsDone: In some Mahayana communities people memorize and chant verses of the Diamond Sutra, and teach them to others, which the sutra names as a way of keeping it.

notes: Section 24 paraphrased, not quoted (Max Müller's wording unverified): check the heaps of the seven precious things as high as the Sumeru mountains in a world system, 'even four lines' kept, recited and explained, and the fractions (not a hundredth part, down to what no number or comparison can reach).
'Gold, silver and the rest' names two of the seven precious things; lists vary between texts, so only these are named. 'Sapta ratna' in the original note: confirm.
Sumeru glossed as 'the great mountain at the center of a world' in Buddhist cosmology; confirm. The train story is the writer's illustration.
